title: Jaw Green
passages:
Kass didn't swing down. One boot on the pedal-rail's frame, the other on the frozen ballast, they breathed through their mouth and said it loud enough for the work light to carry: "J. Renner. That name's on Anza's overlap log. Teodoro countersigned it himself. So the two halves of this ticket on Brill's blank plate — they staple Culvert Nine to Nour's eleven short strikes in a document a desk can actually read."

The wind off the dead pumps didn't care. It tore the words and scattered them across the spur.

Miko didn't look down from the crew box. Her gloved fingers folded the half-torn J. Renner ticket slow and deliberate, like she was putting a letter back in an envelope, and slipped it into her coat's inner pocket. Then her other hand came out holding a second ticket — clean edges, fresh watermark, a name Kass didn't recognize and hadn't seen on any board, any log, any chalk tally in three nodes of riding the line.

"Never touched paper," Miko said. Her voice carried flat over the bearing whine settling in Kass's ears. "Never touched a desk. Never touched a seal."

She tore it clean across the watermark. The sound was small and final in the cold — paper fiber giving way, no ragged edge, no hesitation. Two perfect halves fluttered down into the work light's cone.

Saul didn't move their pencil. Their clipboard stayed pressed to their chest, the M. Varel sheet still open, the graphite tip hovering over a line they'd already written twice.

Brill didn't blink. She stood at the storeroom door with her hand knife at her belt and a child's bowl steady in her other hand, the steam rising from it the only warm thing in the yard. The child — maybe six, maybe seven, wrapped in three coats and a scarf that had seen better winters — watched the paper halves fall.

Kass let their breath out slow. Their knee ached where the bearing had bitten through the packing. "That one doesn't staple anything."

"No," Miko said. She climbed down the rig's ladder rung by rung, boots hitting the deck plate solid. "But it buys the unload. And the eleven cans go into the jaw. And the kid eats."

She landed light, rolled her shoulder, and walked toward the blank door plate without looking at Saul, without looking at Kass. The hand lamp still hung in the crew box window, burning steady against the dark.

Behind her, the blank rig's forward canister gave its fourth cold-cycle bite. The clamp ring sang against the collar, a sound like a bell struck wrong.

Brill didn't reach for the halves right away. She set the child's bowl on the storeroom sill, wiped her knife hand on her coat, and took the two pieces of paper between thumb and forefinger like they were something she'd have to answer for later. The work light threw her shadow long across the deck plate, and the child's face went sharp in the glow — eyes on the ticket halves, then on the eleven canisters sitting in the jaw's steel throat, then back to Brill.

"Three strokes," Brill said. Not to anyone. To the plate.

She knelt in the frozen grit, the knife's blade catching the light. *Scritch. Scritch. Scritch.* Three clean cuts into the blank plate stock, and a fourth — C9, cut deep in the hollow of the crescent. The same mark Kass had seen on their own tally card, the one Nour had struck eleven times short at the Anza jaw. The receiving mark. The mark that said *this node received, this node paid, this node exists.*

Brill stood, wiped the blade again, and held the plate against Kass's tally card in the work light's cone. The two crescents aligned. The chipped edge of the die mark on the card kissed the fresh cut on the plate. A perfect match, or as perfect as cold steel and graphite ever got.

Saul leaned forward. Their pencil didn't move. "First matched crescent since the pumps died," they said. Quiet. Like they were writing it in their head.

The jaw's throat ground open. A sound like rock breaking. The clamp rings released their death grip on the forward canister's collar, and the roller deck shuddered to life under the weight of ten warm canisters. Brill's crew moved without orders — two women and a man in coats patched at the elbows, walking the cans down the deck one by one, boots finding the grating, hands on the cold metal ribs. Steam rose from the canisters where the night air hit them. Protein broth, dense and dark, sloshing behind seals that had held through two hundred kilometers of rattling blank rig.

The eleventh canister didn't move.

It sat at the end of the deck, its collar sealed black. The cold-cycle clamp had bitten deep on the fourth strike, and the metal had flowed into the bite like wax. No reader would open it. No seal would match it now.

Brill didn't look at it long. She turned to the jaw carriage where the reclamation torch sat in its bracket, hose coiled, regulator frozen stiff. "Torch," she called. "Off the carriage. Now."

The reclamation torch coughed blue flame into the frozen air, regulator hissing as Brill cracked the valve. She didn't hesitate — knelt at the eleventh canister's black collar, angled the tip where the clamp ring had bitten deepest, and pulled the trigger. The metal screamed. Not a clean cut. The gasket, cured hard by the cold-cycle bite, didn't part; it *melted* into the kerf, black rubber fusing with steel, sealing the wound as fast as the torch opened it.

Brill swore, low and vicious, and worked the flame sideways. The collar gave way with a wet *pop* of pressure equalizing. Steam erupted, thick and meat-scented, and half the protein broth slumped out scorched — gray at the edges, slack as boiled leather, the good dark red ruined by the heat that had cured the gasket into the cut.

She didn't flinch. Didn't pass the can to anyone else. Just set the torch down on the deck grating, still burning, and caught the lidless bowl the child held out with both hands. Scooped from the scorched half first, ladling thick and silent, the steam curling up into the work light's cone. The child didn't blow on it. Didn't wait. Just ate, shoulders hunched, bowl tilted to catch every drop.

"Skim-fault's mine," Brill said to the deck plate. Her voice carried flat over the roller deck's shudder. "Carry it to whatever desk is standing in the spring."

The crew didn't cheer. Didn't thank her. They moved in around the canister like it was a shift meal at any node — standing, bowls out, eating in the cold slab of storeroom light that spilled from the open throat. A woman with a patched elbow took the second scoop. The man behind her took the third. Nobody spoke. The only sounds were metal spoons on metal bowls, the torch's hiss, the wind off the dead pumps tearing at the steam.

Saul stood at the edge of the light, clipboard braced against their chest, pencil moving. *Torch, one can, spoiled.* Graphite on paper. Clean letters. They wrote it slow, like each stroke cost something, and their jaw worked tight enough that Kass could hear the grind from the pedal-rail saddle.

The M. Varel sheet stayed folded in the clipboard's clip. Unwritten on. Unfinished.

Brill wiped her knife hand on her coat again. Watched her crew eat. Watched the child scrape the bowl clean with fingers that had never known a summer. Didn't look at Saul. Didn't look at Kass. Didn't look at Miko, who stood at the jaw's edge with her hands in her coat pockets, watching the black-sealed collar drip scorched broth onto the deck grating.

"Ten good," Brill said. To no one. To the record. "One spoiled. Eleven struck."

The tally card in Kass's pocket felt heavier than paper had any right to be.

It was the patched-elbow woman again, and this time it wasn't the spoiled can she went for.

The ten good ones were racked inside now, stacked two high along the storeroom wall where the cold couldn't reach the broth, and the crew was working down the last of them by lamplight. The man in the third coat carried the tenth in from the throat, both arms wrapped around its ribs, walking it toward the stack. The woman stood at the rack with her bowl, and while the can was still in his hands — not on the shelf yet, not *stock*, just food walking past her nose — she tipped her thumbnail along the seal lip and took a scoop off the top. Fast. The way you take cream off a churn nobody's watching.

The jaw didn't care which can. A seal was broken in its house. It did the only thing it knew.

The fault lamp — the red bulb in its wire cage over the throat, the one that says *this stock is not clean* — snapped on. The throat began to close.

Not on a can. The seat was empty, the deck clear, ten cans already home. It closed on the man, who was standing in the throat with the tenth in his arms and no time to work out why the walls on either side of his shoulders had started walking together, grinding grit, a hand's width and shutting.

He didn't drop it. That was the part Kass would keep — he turned his shoulder to save the can, and the plate caught the back of his coat and hauled him a half step toward the hinge.

Miko had the pry bar off the carriage hook before the plate could take the second bite. She got the flat steel into the gap at his hip and threw her whole weight down on it. The bar bowed. Held. The throat groaned and stopped, plates trembling a knuckle from his spine and a full can's worth of broth.

"Put it back," Brill said.

The woman stared at her over the bowl.

"The scoop. Off your thumb. Back in the can, all of it, seal and all." Brill never raised her voice; she'd never once needed to. "You skim under a matched crescent, the jaw reads it and shuts, and it don't care what's standing in the gap. Tonight that was a man with dinner in his arms. You want to explain that to him, or you put it back?"

The woman scraped the scoop off her thumbnail with a finger that had started to shake and tipped the whole gray mouthful back into the can. The man didn't move until she had.

The fault lamp held red a moment longer. Then, the seal whole and the can finally on the shelf where it counted, the bulb went dark. The clamp ring let go the deck rail with a clang that rang off the dead pumps. The throat eased back open on Miko's bar, and she pulled it free and hung it on its hook, steam coming off her shoulders in the work light.

The man set the can on the stack with hands that weren't steady and didn't thank a soul. This crew didn't do thanks. But he took his own ration last and slow, thumb nowhere near the lip, and the woman with the patched elbow took hers after him.

Saul hadn't moved the whole while. Clipboard to their chest, the M. Varel sheet still folded under the clip, pencil out. They'd watched the lamp come on and the plates start walking and a station rule they'd spent all evening calling a thief's trick nearly take a man's spine — then watched that same rule stop itself, and a woman's flat order and a loader's back save both the stock and the man, without a cord on anybody's wrist, without one name written down.

Saul looked at the folded sheet for a long time.

Then they shut their mouth around whatever was in it, and kept the pencil still.

The storeroom board was a slab of pitted steel welded to the wall behind the rack, its chalk ledge grooved deep by seasons of names. Forty marks in white, some smudged to ghosts, some sharp as the night they were written. Nour's count from Anza, carried down the line in the dust of eleven canisters and a hand lamp.

Miko pulled a stick of chalk from her coat pocket — not the waxy node issue, the hard stuff loaders buy for themselves — and stepped up to the board. Her glove came off. The cold bit her fingertips, but she didn't hurry.

*Miko Keres.*

Clean letters. Not small. Not hidden. She wrote it under the fortieth name, left a finger's width of space, and set the chalk back in the groove.

The child had finished the bowl and was asleep against the storeroom wall, wrapped in a coat that wasn't hers. Brill didn't look at the board. She took a sawn can lid from the stack — clean cut, edges filed smooth, the kind you make when you've got time and a file and a reason — and pressed it into Miko's palm. The metal was warm from the storeroom's heat. A number was stamped into it: *C9-047*.

"Station loader," Brill said. "Badge catches the reader at the jaw. You unload, you log, you seal. You don't skim, you don't short, you don't let anybody else." She held Miko's eyes. "The door plate's cut now. C9 in the hollow. That's your mark. You break it, you own the fault."

Miko closed her fingers on the lid. The stamped edges bit her palm. "Understood."

Brill nodded once. Turned to the clipboard Saul still held against their chest.

"Sheet," she said.

Saul didn't hand it over. They flipped the clip, unfolded the M. Varel page, and worked the eraser end of their pencil over the name. Graphite dust fell gray on the frozen grit. The paper fibers lifted, thin and stubborn. Saul pressed harder, blew the dust clear, and wrote over the ghost: *Miko Keres*. Same hand. Same pressure. The letters sat clean.

They folded the sheet slow, crease sharp, and clipped it back into the board. The pencil went into the loop. The clipboard came down to their side.

"Turnaround bell," Saul said. Not to anyone. Just the air.

The ridge above the dead spur carried the sound — a hammer on rail, slow and spaced, each stroke eating the last. *Clang. Clang. Clang.* The final stroke hung in the cold, vibrating through the pump station's dead steel, through the storeroom's open throat, through the blank rig sitting locked in the jaw with its hand lamp still burning in the crew box window.

It stopped.

The silence after was heavier than the sound had been.

The silence didn't last. Miko was already moving, gloves back on, walking to the storeroom shelf where the tallow tin sat next to a brick of graphite and a stack of sawn lids. She didn't ask. Just took the pedal-rail's frame from Kass's grip, flipped it onto its stand, and cracked the bearing housing with the same crescent wrench she'd used on the jaw's clamp rings.

"Graphite holds while it's cold," she said, packing the race with fingers that knew the feel of metal on metal. "Tallow holds while it's warm. Together they lie to each other about the middle." She cut a washer from a fresh lid — *snick, snick* — and seated it in the housing groove, the stamped number *C9-047* facing out like a joke. "Past the second culvert, this cooks again. You walk the last stretch on a leg that already has opinions."

Kass watched from the saddle, knee throbbing in time with the wind. "Your honesty is shit timing."

"Your bearing is shit timing." Miko torqued the cap bolt, wiped her hands on her coat, and handed the rail back. "Ride while it rolls. Walk when it don't. The node's still there either way."

Brill stood at the tally card nailed to the door frame, the child's empty bowl at her feet. She took a cold chisel and a hammer from the shelf, set the chisel's tip on the eleventh notch — the one Nour had left hollow at Anza — and struck. *Clack.* The steel yielded a clean V. She moved to the tenth. *Clack.* Ninth. *Clack.* Down the line, eleven strikes, eleven notches full, the graphite dust from Kass's card settling in the fresh cuts like snow in boot prints.

Then she set the chisel beside the notches, angled it, and cut *C9* in steel beside them. Deep. Deliberate. The same mark on the door plate. The same mark on Miko's badge. A node's name, witnessed in metal.

Kass took the chalk from their pocket and stepped to the jaw plate where Brill had cut the receiving crescent. The blank rig sat locked in the throat, hand lamp still burning in the crew box window, eleven canisters unloaded and the deck empty. They wrote: *ANZA SALVAGE — UNCLAIMED — 11 CANISTERS RECEIVED C9*. The chalk dusted their fingers white.

Miko climbed the rig's ladder one last time, retrieved the hand lamp from the crew box, and carried it down. She hung it on a nail inside the storeroom door, the hook Brill had driven years ago for the night lantern. The flame caught the glass, threw warm light across the sackcloth coats hanging beside it, the child's asleep face, the stack of ten good cans and one scorched.

"Stays," Miko said. "For the next unload."

Brill didn't answer. Just nodded at the pedal-rail.

Kass swung onto the frame, bad knee locking, good boot finding the pedal. The bearing turned over smooth and quiet, the graphite-tallow lie holding its breath. They didn't look back at the storeroom board where *Miko Keres* sat clean under forty ghosts. Didn't look at the tally card with eleven full notches and a node's name cut in steel. Didn't look at the blank rig sleeping in the jaw under a hand lamp's watch.

The pedal-rail pulled out north, bearing singing low, the dead pumps fading behind them, the ridge swallowing the light.
